vignette:
William sits in the chair across from me, his hands resting motionless on his thighs, his posture rigid. He is sixty-nine years old, a financial analyst who spent forty-two years with the same firm, but he retired six months ago-not by choice. He tells me that the numbers no longer hold meaning for him. He used to see patterns in market data the way other people see faces in a crowd, but now the columns blur. "I stare at the screen and my mind goes blank," he says, his voice flat.

The event that changed everything happened three years ago, on a Tuesday evening in November. His wife, Carol, had been feeling tired for weeks, but they attributed it to age. She was seventy-one, active, still gardening. That night, she stood up from the dinner table, touched her chest, and said, "Bill, something's wrong." He watched her face go pale, saw her hand grip the back of the chair, and then she collapsed. He called 911 and performed CPR until the paramedics arrived, but he knew-even as he pressed on her sternum, counting compressions-that she was gone. The emergency room doctor said it was a massive coronary. No warning. No chance.

In the months that followed, William tried to return to work. He was a senior analyst, respected for his precision and calm under pressure. But the calm had shattered. He found himself jolting at the sound of a phone ringing, his heart hammering as if the call would bring news of another death. He would walk into a meeting and catch the faint scent of Carol's perfume on someone's coat, and suddenly he was back in the kitchen, her body crumpled on the linoleum, the feel of her ribs cracking under his hands. He began to avoid the office breakroom because it smelled like the hospital. He stopped attending team lunches because they reminded him of the last meal they had together-roast chicken and a glass of red wine she never finished.

His supervisors noticed the decline. They offered him a reduced workload, but William could not focus. He would catch himself staring at columns of quarterly earnings, unblinking, for twenty minutes. The numbers felt like hieroglyphics. He started making small errors-transposing digits, missing deadlines-and he knew he was failing. Six months ago, he accepted an early retirement package. He tells me this without emotion, as if reciting a quarterly report that happened to someone else.

Now he lives alone in the house where Carol died. He has not moved a single item in the living room. Her knitting basket sits beside the armchair, half a scarf still on the needles. He cannot bring himself to throw it away, but he also cannot sit in that chair. He avoids the kitchen after dark. At night, he sleeps on the couch in the den, with the television on low-not to watch, but to drown out the silence. He says he hasn't slept more than three hours in a stretch since she died. When he closes his eyes, he sees her face, hears her last words. Sometimes he wakes in a cold sweat, convinced he is still pressing on her chest.

William no longer calls his daughter in California. He used to talk to her every Sunday, but now he lets the calls go to voicemail. He tells me he doesn't want to burden her with his grief, but I see the way he flinches when the phone rings-that same jolt, that same flashback. He stopped going to the grocery store because the fluorescent lights remind him of the hospital corridor. He eats mostly canned soup and crackers, whatever doesn't require a trip to the kitchen.

He is a man who made a career out of predicting risk, but he could not foresee this. He tells me, "I used to believe that if I planned carefully, I could control things. Now I know that's a lie." He looks older than his sixty-nine years, his shoulders hunched, his eyes fixed on a spot on the carpet. He came to therapy because his daughter threatened to drive across the country and move in with him if he didn't. He says he doesn't expect me to fix anything. But every session, he arrives ten minutes early, and he stays a few minutes after we finish, as if the room itself is a kind of shelter from the world that took his wife.
